parole.significato: leading, leader
parole.testo: From Late Latin -archa, from Latin -archēs, from Ancient Greek -άρχης (-árkhēs), from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule, government”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ergʰ- (“to begin, rule, command”).

parole.significato: Noun suffix that denotes a condition, action, or process.
parole.testo: French form of -esis, from Late Latin -esia, from -ēsis, from Ancient Greek -ησις (-ēsis), from -σις (-sis).

parole.significato: worship of
parole.testo: From Late Latin latria, from Ancient Greek λατρεία (latreía, “service; worship”).

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives indicating a fear of a specific thing.
parole.testo: From -phobia (from Late Latin -phobia, from Koine Greek -φοβία (-phobía), from φόβος (phóbos, “fear”)) + -ic.

parole.significato: To blind by holding a red-hot metal rod or plate before the eyes
parole.testo: From Late Latin abacinātus, perfect passive participle of abacinō; possibly formed from ab (“off”) + bacīnum (“a basin”) or bacīnus. Probably cognate with modern Italian abbacinare (“to dazzle”).

parole.significato: One who steals and drives away cattle or beasts by herds or droves; a cattle rustler.
parole.testo: From Late Latin abactor (“cattle rustler”), from abigō (“drive away”); from ab (“from, away from”) + agō (“drive”).

parole.significato: An informer; a criminal who informs on other criminals to the authorities.
parole.testo: UK C19. From Abaddon, from Middle English, from Late Latin, from Ancient Greek Ἀβαδδών (Abaddṓn, “Abaddon”), from Hebrew אבדון (ābaddōn, “destruction, abyss”), from אבד (ābad, “to be lost, to perish”).

parole.significato: The dignity, estate, term, or jurisdiction of an abbot or abbess.
parole.testo: From Middle English abbathie, from Late Latin abbātia, from abbās, abbātis (“abbot”). Doublet of abbey and Opatija.

parole.significato: Someone who is learning the alphabet.
parole.testo: From Late Latin abecedarius (from the first four letters of the Latin alphabet + -arius). Equivalent to abecedary + -an. Compare abecedary.

parole.significato: Referring to the alphabet; alphabetical; related to or resembling an abecedarius; abecedarian.
parole.testo: From Late Latin abecedārius. Doublet of abecedarius.

parole.significato: To eradicate; to pull up by the roots.
parole.testo: From Late Latin aberuncare, from Latin averruncare.

parole.significato: The weaning of a child from the breast, or of young animals from their dam.
parole.testo: From Middle English ablactacioun from Late Latin ablactatio, ablactō (“to wean”) from ab (“without”) + lacto (“suckle”), from lac (“milk”); equivalent to ab- + lactation.

parole.significato: A carrying or taking away; removal.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English ablacioun (“removal”), from Late Latin ablātiō (“a taking away”), from auferō (“to take away, carry off, withdraw, remove”) + -tiō (“-tion”, nominal suffix). Doublet of ablatio. Compare French ablation. By surface analysis, ablat(e) + -ion.

parole.significato: That which is washed off.
parole.testo: From Late Latin abluvio. See abluent.

parole.significato: One who abnegates, denies, or rejects.
parole.testo: From Late Latin abnegator, from abnegatus. Equivalent to abnegate + -or.

parole.significato: Abominable; detested.
parole.testo: First attested in 1644. Perhaps a back-formation from abomination. Alternatively, perhaps from Late Latin abōminātus, past participle of abōminarī (“to deprecate as an ill omen”), from ab + ominari (“to forebode, presage”), from omen.

parole.significato: A use of the mystical term ‘abracadabra’, supposed to work as part of a healing charm or a magical spell; any spell or…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin abracadabra.

parole.significato: A gem engraved with the word Abrasax or Abraxas.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin Abrasax, from Ancient Greek ἀβραξάς (abraxás) or ἀβρασάξ (abrasáx), possibly from the numerical value of the Greek letters, which is 365.

parole.significato: Pertaining to absence.
parole.testo: From Late Latin absentaneus. See absent.

parole.significato: Hell; the bottomless pit; primeval chaos; a confined subterranean ocean.
parole.testo: From Middle English abissus, from Late Latin abyssus (“a bottomless gulf”), from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος (ábussos, “bottomless”, from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + βυσσός (bussós, “deep place”)), from βυθός (buthós, “deep place”). Displaced native Old English neowolnes.

parole.significato: A birth defect in which the heart is absent
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin acardia, formed on Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “-less”) + κᾰρδῐ́ᾱ (kărdĭ́ā, “heart”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, suffix forming abstract nouns). Equivalent to a- + -cardia.

parole.significato: Designating a line of verse having the required number of syllables in the last foot
parole.testo: From Late Latin acatalēcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκατάληκτος (akatálēktos, “leaving off”).

parole.significato: A more distinct or prominent form.
parole.testo: From Late Latin accentuatio. Compare French accentuation. Equivalent to accentuate + -ion.

parole.significato: The quality of being accessible, or of admitting approach; receptiveness.
parole.testo: From accessible + -ity, after Late Latin accessibilitas, from Latin accessibilis.

parole.significato: Continuous growth; an accretion.
parole.testo: From Late Latin accrescentia. Compare Italian accrescente.

parole.significato: A group of individuals who didn't adhear to the condemnation of Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus (431 CE).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin acephalus, from Ancient Greek ἀκέφαλος (aképhalos, “headless”), apparently referring to the various movements’ refusals to accept the decisions of church councils.

parole.significato: A radical Monophysite in the era after the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin acephalus + -ite, from Ancient Greek ἀκέφαλος (aképhalos, “headless”), apparently referring to the movement’s refusal to accept the decisions of church councils.

parole.significato: a follower of an Acephali movement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin acephalus + -ite, from Ancient Greek ἀκέφαλος (aképhalos, “headless”)

parole.significato: The quality of being acetous; sourness.
parole.testo: acetous + -ity as -osity; from Late Latin acetositas.

parole.significato: To quiet.
parole.testo: From Late Latin acquietare, from Latin ad + quies (“rest”). Equivalent to a- + quiet. Doublet of acquit. See also quiet and aquiesce.

parole.significato: Lack of self-control; excess, intemperance; also, irregular or unruly behaviour.

parole.significato: Able to be acted on; able to be used as the basis for taking action.
parole.testo: From action + -able. Compare Late Latin actionabilis. See action.

parole.significato: The act or acts constituting a criminal offense, as distinguished from the intentions or state of mind of the perpetrat…
parole.testo: From Late Latin āctus reus (“guilty act”), from Latin āctus (“act”) + reus (“guilty”); after Late Latin and English mens rea.

parole.significato: Pertaining to addition; that can be, or has been, added.
parole.testo: From Late Latin additivus, from the participial stem of Latin addere (“to add”).

parole.significato: A form of hyperbole that uses exaggeration so magnified as to express impossibility; an instance of such hyperbole.

parole.significato: The bleak, a small European fish with silvery scales.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin alburnus. Cognate with alburnum and auburn.

parole.significato: A universal solvent sought by the alchemists.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin alcahest, apparently coined by Paracelsus as a pseudo-Arabism.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or consisting of an alleluia.
parole.testo: From Late Latin alleluiaticus, from Latin alleluia.

parole.significato: To reduce or lessen the severity of a pain or difficulty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin alleviatus, past participle of alleviāre (“to lighten; to alleviate”). By surface analysis, al- + Latin lev- + -i- + -ate.

parole.significato: A raised platform in an early Christian church, as well as in the Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, and Eastern Cath…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ambō, from Ancient Greek ἄμβων (ámbōn).

parole.significato: For the purpose of amending or correction.
parole.testo: From Late Latin ēmendātōrius (with a- for e- from amend).

parole.significato: Showing friendliness or goodwill.
parole.testo: From Middle English amicable (“agreeable; pleasant”), from Late Latin amīcābilis (“friendly”). Doublet of amiable.

parole.significato: An ecclesiastical vestment like the chasuble.
parole.testo: From Late Latin amphibalus (“cloak”), from unattested Ancient Greek *ἀμφίβαλος (*amphíbalos), from ἀμφιβάλλω (amphibállō, “put on”).

parole.significato: The inability to comprehend or respond to music.
parole.testo: From Late Latin amusia, from Ancient Greek ἀμουσία (amousía, “without harmony”), from ἄμουσος (ámousos, “without song”). The Muses were the nine daughters of Zeus and the goddesses of arts and sciences.

parole.significato: Synonym of anacoluthon.
parole.testo: From Late Latin anacolūthon, from Ancient Greek ἀνακόλουθον (anakólouthon).

parole.significato: sinuous, twisty, winding.
parole.testo: From Late Latin anfractuosus, from Latin anfractus (“bend, curve”).

parole.significato: To make, or to become, angular.

parole.testo: From Middle English annexion, from Late Latin annexiō.

parole.significato: Happening once every year.
parole.testo: First attested around 1382, borrowed from Late Latin annuālem, annuālis, related to Latin annālis, adjective form of annus (“year”). Used to categorize plants since 1710.

parole.significato: Deviating from the normal; marked by incongruity or contradiction; aberrant or abnormal.
parole.testo: From Late Latin anōmalos, from Ancient Greek ἀνώμᾰλος (anṓmălos).

parole.significato: Lacking a name; not named, for example an animal not assigned to any species .
parole.testo: Borrowed into English around 1600 from Late Latin anonymus, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓νώνῠμος (ănṓnŭmos, “without name”), from ᾰ̓ν- (ăn-, “un-”) with ὄνῠμᾰ (ónŭmă), Aeolic and Doric dialectal form of ὄνομᾰ (ónomă, “name”). English equivalent anonym + -ous, its full etymology being an- + -onym + -ous.

parole.testo: From Late Latin antichresis, from Ancient Greek ἀντίχρησις (antíkhrēsis).

parole.significato: Use of a word or phrase in a sense opposite of its literal meaning, especially for ironic or humorous effect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin antiphrasis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀντίφρασις (antíphrasis) (< phrazein "declare").

parole.significato: The process of becoming antique or obsolete.
parole.testo: From Late Latin antīquātiō, antīquātiōnem, noun of action from past-participle stem of antīquāre. English antique + -ation.

parole.significato: A silver coin used during the Roman Empire, equal to two denarii.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Antōnīniānus (“pertaining to Antoninus”). Speculatively named in modern times after an Antoninus mentioned in the Augustan History, after whom some silver coins were said to be named. However, it is not known what this coin was called in antiquity.

parole.significato: The loss or omission of the last vowel in a word, together with any consonants that follow it.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin apocopē, derived from Ancient Greek ἀποκοπή (apokopḗ), ἀποκόπτω (apokóptō, “cut off”).

parole.significato: Something, as a writing, that is of doubtful authorship or authority (formerly also used attributively).

parole.significato: The consequential clause in a conditional sentence.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin apodosis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀπόδοσις (apódosis).

parole.significato: A systematic defense of a position, or of religious or occult doctrine.
parole.testo: From Late Latin apologia, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογία (apología, “a speech in defense”), from ἀπολογοῦμαι (apologoûmai, “I speak in one's defense”), from ἀπόλογος (apólogos, “an account, story”), from ἀπό (apó, “from, off”) (see apo-) + λόγος (lógos, “speech”) + -ics.

parole.significato: An allusion to something by denying that it will be mentioned.
parole.testo: Via Late Latin apophasis from Ancient Greek ἀπόφασις (apóphasis, “denial, negation”) from ἀπο- (apo-, “away, from, off”) + φάσις (phásis, “statement, proposition”) from φημί (phēmí, “to speak”) from Proto-Hellenic *pʰā́mā from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂; whence Latin fārī, cognate to fame, fable.

parole.significato: Guilty of apostasy.
parole.testo: From Late Latin apostata, from Ancient Greek ἀποστάτης (apostátēs, “rebel”), from ἀφίστημι (aphístēmi, “to withdraw, revolt”), from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).

parole.significato: The office, or responsibilities of an apostle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin apostolātus. By surface analysis, apostle + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office). Doublet of apostolado.

parole.significato: To appear magically; to teleport to or from a place.
parole.testo: From Late Latin apparēre (“to appear”), as of a servant who appears on being summoned. A back-formation from apparition.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an appellative noun or common noun.
parole.testo: From the Late Latin appellātīvus, from the stem appella- (“to call”), with the adjectival suffix -ive.

parole.significato: A person to whom the authority to settle or judge a dispute is delegated.
parole.testo: From Middle English arbitrator, from Late Latin arbitrātor, from arbitror.

parole.significato: A smell; especially a pleasant, spicy or fragrant one.
parole.testo: From Late Latin arōmata (“spices”) (or arōma (“spice”)), from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma, “seasoning, spicy and/or fragrant smell”).

parole.significato: The permanent fixation of a joint in a contracted position.
parole.testo: From arthro- (“joint”) + gryposis (“hooking, abnormal curvature”), from Late Latin grȳpōsis (“hooking”) (from grȳpus (“hook-nosed”)), from Ancient Greek γρυπῶσις (grupôsis, “hooking”), from γρύπεσθαι (grúpesthai, “become hooked”), from γρύπος (grúpos, “hook-nosed”).

parole.significato: A member of a sect in the primitive church who celebrated the Lord's Supper with bread and cheese.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Artotyritae, plural, from Ancient Greek ἄρτος (ártos, “loaf”) + τυρός (turós, “cheese”).

parole.significato: self-discipline, particularly as a religious observance; asceticism.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin ascesis, or directly from its etymon, Ancient Greek ἄσκησις (áskēsis, “exercise, training”), from ἀσκέω (askéō, “to exercise, practise, train”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, suffix forming abstract nouns or nouns of action, result or process).

parole.significato: The structure that unites the ascidiozooids in a compound ascidian.
parole.testo: From Late Latin. See ascidium.

parole.significato: To pave with asphalt.
parole.testo: From Late Latin asphaltum, from Ancient Greek ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt, bitumen”). Displaced native Old English eorþtyrewa (literally, "earth-tar").

parole.significato: Relating to the former genus Astraea or the family Astraeidae.
parole.testo: From Late Latin astraeus or similar, from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (astḗr, “star”).

parole.significato: Relating to or resembling the stars; starry.
parole.testo: From Late Latin astrālis, from Latin astrum (“star”), from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”).

parole.significato: To be tedious to; to exhaust.
parole.testo: From (the stem of) Late Latin attaediāre.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a large hall.
parole.testo: From stem of Late Latin aularis (from Latin aula (“a hall”), from Ancient Greek αὐλά (aulá)) + -ian.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the ear.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, borrowed from Late Latin auriculāris, from auricula (“the external ear; the ear”) + -āris (“-ar”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to auricle + -ar. Doublet of auricularis.

parole.significato: Embroidered or decorated with gold.
parole.testo: From Late Latin auriphrigiatus; Latin aurum (“gold”) + Late Latin phrygiare (“to adorn with Phrygian needlework, or with embroidery”); perhaps corrupted from some other word.

parole.significato: time for a judge to consider a case and reach a decision.
parole.testo: From Late Latin avizō (“consider”), from Latin a + vīsō (“look carefully”).

parole.significato: Unleavened bread used in Jewish or Christian religious contexts.
parole.testo: From Late Latin azyma, from the adjective azymus (“unleavened”), from Ancient Greek ἄζυμος (ázumos).

parole.significato: A tax, similar to murage, paid for the upkeep of a barbican.

parole.significato: Order of battle; disposition or arrangement of troops or of a naval force, ready for action.

parole.significato: To treat or impregnate with bitumen.

parole.significato: A round mass of something, especially of chewed food in the mouth or alimentary canal.

parole.significato: Concise speech; laconism.

parole.testo: From Late Latin brachiologia, from Ancient Greek βραχύς (brakhús, “short”) + -λογία (-logía, “speech”); compare brachylogy.

parole.significato: A tubular glass or plastic bead sewn onto clothes as a decorative trim.

parole.significato: A collection of papal bulls.
parole.testo: From Late Latin bullarium: compare French bullairie.

parole.significato: Resembling a bulla or blister; inflated; blistered; bulliform.

parole.significato: A lung disease, caused by exposure to cotton dust in inadequately ventilated working environments.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Byzantium.

parole.significato: A systemic wasting of muscle tissue, with or without loss of fat mass, that accompanies a chronic disease.
parole.testo: From Late Latin cachexia or French cachexie, from Ancient Greek καχεξία (kakhexía), from κακός (kakós, “bad; injurious”) + ἕξῐς (héxĭs, “act of having; habit or state of body”) (ultimately from ἔχω (ékhō, “to have”)) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă, suffix added to adjectives to form abstract nouns).

parole.significato: Possessing the traits of calumny.
parole.testo: From Late Latin calumniōsus.

parole.significato: A life-size representation of the crucifixion of Jesus Christ on a piece of raised ground.
parole.testo: From Late Latin calvāria (“skull”). Doublet of calavera and calvaria.

parole.significato: The half-demon offspring of either an incubus and a female human or a succubus and a male human.
parole.testo: From Late Latin cambio (“I exchange”). Doublet of change.

parole.significato: A layer of cells between the xylem and the phloem that is responsible for the secondary growth of roots and stems.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin cambium (“a change”), from Gaulish. Doublet of change.

parole.significato: A 12th-century English game somewhat similar to golf in that it was played with a wooden ball similar to a golf ball.

parole.significato: canonical

parole.significato: An act passed in a chapter.

parole.significato: A summary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin capitulum (“chapter”) (diminutive of Latin caput (“head”)).

parole.significato: The thick wall on the proximal side of the corpus of a pollen grain.

parole.significato: One who is holding a captive or captives.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin captor, from Latin capiō. English usage began around 1688.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to imprisonment or a prison.

parole.significato: Embodied in, or having, flesh (as opposed to just a spirit etc.).
parole.testo: From Late Latin carnātus (“fleshy”), from oblique stem of Latin carō, carnis (“meat, flesh”) + -ātus (whence -ate).

parole.significato: A form of land taxation that replaced Danegeld in twelfth-century England.
parole.testo: From Late Latin carrucagium, from carruca (“plough”); compare tillage.

parole.significato: To render void; to undo or annul.
parole.testo: From Late Latin cassare. See cass.

parole.significato: categorical

parole.significato: The degree to which something, such as a plant or neuron, has a well-formed main stem.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or being a cause of something; causing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin causalis, from Latin causa (“cause”), equivalent to cause + -al, see cause.

parole.significato: A cellar used for storage in an abbey.

parole.significato: Synonym of century: A period of 100 years.

parole.significato: Filled with chaos.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, written for, or performed by a choir or a chorus.

parole.significato: The protective and nutritive membrane in higher vertebrates that attaches the fetus to the uterus.

parole.significato: The thick semifluid mass of partly digested food that is passed from the stomach to the duodenum.
parole.testo: From Late Latin chymus, from Ancient Greek χυμός (khumós, “juice”).

parole.significato: The act of shutting up or confining; confinement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin clausūra, from Latin clausus. See closure and cloture, which are doublets.

parole.significato: A harpsichord in which the soundboard and strings are mounted vertically facing the player.

parole.significato: Of or relating to clerks or their work.
parole.testo: From Late Latin clēricālis (“clerical”), from clēricus (“clergyman, priest”).

parole.significato: Belonging to the same age, era or period; coeval or contemporary.

parole.significato: Of the same age or era; contemporary.
parole.testo: From Late Latin coaevus, from Latin con- (“equal”) + aevum (“age”).

parole.significato: A groove sometimes occurring on grains of pollen
parole.testo: From Late Latin colpus (“hollow space, pocket”), from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos, “hollow space, pocket”).

parole.significato: Having short clauses or sentences, often separated with commas
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin commaticus, from Ancient Greek κομματικός (kommatikós). See comma.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or suitable for communication.

parole.significato: To unite or hold together.

parole.significato: To sum or collect together.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin compendiātus, perfect passive participle of compendiō (“to shorten”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from compendium.

parole.significato: that compensates for something; compensatory

parole.significato: The ability to perform some task; competence.
parole.testo: From Late Latin competentia. Doublet of competence.

parole.significato: A feeling of contented self-satisfaction, especially when unaware of upcoming trouble.
parole.testo: Late Middle English complacence, from Late Latin complacentia. Compare French complaisance.

parole.significato: Compulsatory; employing force or constraint.
parole.testo: From Late Latin compulsāt-, participial stem of compulsāre, intensitive form of Latin compellere (“to compel”).

parole.significato: Required; obligatory; mandatory.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin compulsorius, from Latin compulsus. Displaced native Old English ġenīedelīċ.

parole.significato: Subject to conditions.

parole.significato: The act or method of controlling or directing.

parole.significato: Relating to, or of the nature of confections or their production.

parole.significato: A manual or guide to making confession.
parole.testo: From Late Latin confessionarium.

parole.significato: A blowing or fusing together, as of many instruments in a concert, or of many fires in a foundry.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin cōnflātiō, from Latin cōnflātus. By surface analysis, conflate + -ion.

parole.significato: The act of combining that occurs where two rivers meet.
parole.testo: From late Middle English confluence, from Late Latin cōnfluentia (“a flowing together, conflux”), from cōnfluēns (present participle of cōnfluō (“to flow or run together”)) + -ia (nominal suffix).

parole.significato: The act of constricting, the state of being constricted, or something that constricts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin constrictio, constrictionis, from Latin constringo.

parole.significato: A translation.
parole.testo: From Middle English construen, from Late Latin construo, construere (“to relate grammatically”), from Latin construo (“pile together”); doublet of construct.

parole.significato: Having the same bounds or extent; coterminous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin conterminātus, perfect passive participle of conterminō (“to border upon”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from conterminus (“conterminous”), from con- + terminus (“border”).

parole.significato: A person or company that builds or improves buildings or structures.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin contractor, from Latin contract-, stem of contractus + -tor. First attested in the 16th century.

parole.significato: That contradicts something, such as an argument.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin contradictorius, from Latin contradico. Equivalent to contradict + -ory.

parole.significato: To work or act together, especially for a common purpose or benefit.
parole.testo: Originated 1595–1605 from Late Latin cooperātus, perfect passive participle of cooperor (“to work with”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more. Equivalent to co- + operate. Displaced native Old English efnwyrċan.

parole.testo: From Middle English, from Late Latin corōllārium (“money paid for a garland; gift, gratuity, corollary; consequence, deduction”), from corōlla (“small garland”), diminutive of corōna (“crown”).

parole.significato: The act of corroborating, strengthening, or confirming; addition of strength; confirmation.
parole.testo: From Middle English corroboracioun, borrowed from Late Latin corrōborātiō (“strengthening”).

parole.significato: A cobweb-like annulus on certain types of mushroom.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin cōrtīna (“curtain”). Doublet of curtain.

parole.significato: Tending to create things, or having the ability to create; often, excellently, in a novel fashion, or any or all of the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin creativus, from Latin creō. Equivalent to create + -ive. Displaced native Old English orþanclīċ.

parole.significato: A spinning organ having many fine pores, situated in front of the spinners in some araneomorph spiders.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin cribellum, diminutive of Latin cribrum (“sieve”).

parole.significato: An execution by being nailed or tied to an upright cross and left to hang there until dead.
parole.testo: From Middle English crucifixioun, from Late Latin noun of process crucifīxiō, from perfect passive participle crucifīxus (“fixed to a cross”), from crux (“cross”) + fīgō.

parole.significato: Having hidden (unapparent) meaning.

parole.significato: A concave vessel for drinking, usually made of opaque material (as opposed to a glass) and with a handle.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin custumale (adjective, neuter form of custumalis), used as an adjectival noun. Attested to 1576.

parole.significato: To make worse; to make inferior in quality or value; to impair.

parole.significato: A gap or space between two adjacent teeth, especially the upper front incisors (in humans).

parole.significato: Relating to or produced by a flood or deluge.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin dīluviālis.

parole.significato: The act of dividing into halves.

parole.significato: A lack of continuity, regularity or sequence; a break or gap.

parole.significato: Marking distinction or separation.

parole.significato: The act of dissipating or dispersing; a state of dispersion or separation; dispersion; waste.

parole.significato: To explain or interpret docetically.

parole.significato: To treat something as dogma.

parole.significato: Doubtfulness.

parole.significato: A ruler or governor, especially a hereditary ruler or someone who founded or is part of a dynasty.

parole.significato: Capable of being eaten without harm; suitable for consumption; innocuous to humans.

parole.significato: The mucous membrane that lines the uterus in mammals and in which fertilized eggs are implanted.

parole.significato: A time period of indeterminate length, generally more than one year.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin aera.

parole.significato: Ethnic.

parole.significato: A fabrication, fantasy, invention; something fictitious.
parole.testo: From Late Latin figmentum (“anything made, a fiction”), from fingō (“make, form, feign”); see fiction, feign, feint.

parole.significato: The relation of a son to a father; sonship
parole.testo: From Late Latin filietatem, from filius (“son”).

parole.significato: A series of threads or other projections resembling a fringe.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin fimbria (“a border, fringe”), from Latin fimbriae (“fibers, threads, fringe”). Doublet of fringe.

parole.significato: Covered or growing in wooly tufts
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin floccosus.

parole.significato: The quality of smoothness of flow.
parole.testo: From Late Latin fluentia, equivalent to fluent + -cy. Cognate with French fluence.

parole.significato: The act of fomenting; the application of warm, soft, medicinal substances, as for the purpose of easing pain by relaxin…
parole.testo: From Middle English fōmentāciǒun (“act of fomenting; lotion or poultice applied to a diseased part of the body”), from Late Latin fōmentātiō, fōmentātiōnem, from fōmentāre (from fōmentum (“lotion; compress, poultice; warm application; fomentation”), from foveō (“to warm, keep warm; to cherish, nurtu

parole.significato: Having foramina or openings.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin forāminātus, from forāmen + -ātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To renounce a legal title to a further share of paternal inheritance.
parole.testo: From Late Latin forisfamiliatus, past participle of forisfamiliare (“to forisfamiliate”).

parole.significato: A formative faculty.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin fōrmātrīx. By surface analysis, form + -ate + -trix.

parole.significato: Serving to express repetition of an action.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English frequentatyf, from Late Latin frequentātīvus, from Latin frequentāre (“to do or use often”), from frequēns (“often, regular, constant, repeated, assiduous”) + -ō. By surface analysis, frequent + -ative.

parole.significato: Resembling or pertaining to grain, especially wheat.
parole.testo: From Late Latin frumentaceus, from Latin frumentum (“grain”), from the root of frux (“fruit”).

parole.significato: Fulvous; tawny-coloured.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin fulvidus, from fulvus.

parole.significato: A basic truth, elementary concept, principle, rule, or law. An individual fundamental will often serve as a building bl…
parole.testo: From Middle English foundamental, fundamental, from Late Latin fundāmentālis, from Latin fundāmentum (“foundation”), from fundō (“to lay the foundation (of something), to found”), from fundus (“bottom”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn. By surface analysis, fundament + -al.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a funeral.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin fūnerārius, from Latin funus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the ancient city of Gadara (near modern-day Umm Qais, in Jordan).
parole.testo: From the Late Latin Gadarēnus, from the Ancient Greek Γαδαρηνός (Gadarēnós, “inhabitant of Gadara”), from Γάδαρα (Gádara, “Gadara”, now “Umm Qais”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to gems.
parole.testo: From Late Latin gemmarius.

parole.significato: The placement of someone's penis between another person's knees.
parole.testo: Macaronic from Late Latin genu (“knee”) + phallus (“penis”) + -ation.

parole.significato: A mathematician who specializes in geometry.
parole.testo: From Middle English gemeter, geometer, ultimately from Late Latin geōmetrēs, from Ancient Greek γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) + μετρέω (metréō, “to measure”).

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Gerasa
parole.testo: From the Late Latin Gerasēnus, Gergesēnus, from the Ancient Greek Γερασηνός (Gerasēnós), Γεργεσηνός (Gergesēnós), from Γέρασα (Gérasa), Γέργεσα (Gérgesa). By surface analysis, Gerasa + -ene.

parole.significato: A hinge joint.
parole.testo: From Late Latin, from Ancient Greek γίγγλυμος (gínglumos, “hinge”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or composed of glands; glandular, glandulose.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin glandulōsus, from Latin glandula. By surface analysis, glandule + -ous.

parole.significato: Relating to goth music or people.
parole.testo: From gothic rock, first used by John Stickney in reference to The Doors in 1967 and used by the late 1970s to describe the musical scene that gave rise to the goth subculture, both from a supposed aesthetic similarity to dark and moody 19th century gothic fiction and earlier gothic art and architect

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Goths or their language.
parole.testo: From Late Latin gothicus (“Gothic, barbaric”), from Ancient Greek Γοτθικός (Gotthikós), from Ancient Greek Γότθοι (Gótthoi, “Goths”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”), proposed to derive from unattested Gothic *𐌲𐌿𐍄𐌰 (*guta). Equivalent to Goth + -ic. The various usages of the adjective are introduced nearly si

parole.significato: Adoption of Greek naming and/or the Greek language.
parole.testo: An adaptation of the Late Latin Graecitās (“the Greek language”).

parole.significato: Synonym of grandiloquence.
parole.testo: Probably partly from Late Latin grandiloquium, and partly (especially in later use) an alteration of grandiloquence after other words in -loquy. By surface analysis, grand + -i- + -loquy.

parole.significato: Consisting of, or resembling, granules or grains.
parole.testo: From Late Latin grānulum (“granule, little grain”), diminutive of Latin grānum (“grain, seed”), + -ar. By surface analysis, granule + -ar. Compare French granulaire.

parole.significato: A grievance complained of.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin gravāmen (“physical inconvenience”) and Medieval Latin gravāmen (“grievance”), from Latin gravāre + -men (suffix forming neuter nouns of the third declension). Gravāre is the present active infinitive of gravō (“to burden, weigh down; to oppress”), from gravis (“hea

parole.significato: Abnormal curvature or hooked appearance.
parole.testo: From Late Latin grȳpōsis (“hooking”) (from grȳpus (“hook-nosed”)), from Ancient Greek γρυπῶσις (grupôsis, “hooking”), from γρύπεσθαι (grúpesthai, “become hooked”), from γρύπος (grúpos, “hook-nosed”).

parole.significato: Excessive appetite; greed, gluttony.
parole.testo: From Late Latin gulōsitātem, from gulōsus (“gluttonous”).

parole.significato: Qualified or entitled.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin habilitātus, past participle of habilitāre (“to enable”).

parole.significato: The dugong.
parole.testo: From Late Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek ἅλς (háls, “sea”) + κόρη (kórē, “girl, maiden”).

parole.significato: A big toe.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hallux, from Latin allus, hallus.

parole.significato: A group of seven.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hebdomada (“number seven; group of seven; seven days”), hebdomas (“number seven; seven days; seventh day”), from Ancient Greek ἑβδομάς (hebdomás, “group of seven, especially seven days or seven years”), from ἕβδομος (hébdomos, “seventh”) + -ᾰ́ς (-ắs, suffix forming abstract nouns of

parole.significato: hebdomadal
parole.testo: From Late Latin hebdomadārius, from hebdomas (“week”).

parole.significato: Mental lethargy or dullness.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hebetūdō.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Hebrew people, language, or culture.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Ebrayk, Hebrak, Hebrayke, a learned borrowing from Late Latin hebraicus, borrowed from Byzantine Greek Ἑβρᾰῐ̈κός (Hebrăĭ̈kós), from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos, “Hebrew”). By surface analysis, Hebra- + -ic.

parole.significato: Texts or artifacts containing Hebrew writing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin hebraica, neuter plural of hebraicus (“Hebrew”), from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos), from Hebrew עִבְרִי (ʿiḇrī, “Hebrew”) (likely through Aramaic עִבְרַי (ʿiḇray, “Hebrew”)), traditionally from עֵבֶר ('éver, “Eber”), the ancestor of the Israelites. By surface an

parole.significato: An insatiable and obsessive bookworm (“avid book reader”).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin helluō librōrum (“glutton of books”), from Latin helluō (“glutton; squanderer”) + librōrum (“of books”). Helluō is derived from helluārī + -ō (suffix forming masculine agent nouns, nicknames, and other designations); helluārī is the present active infinitive of hell

parole.significato: A headache affecting one side of the head.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hemicrania (“pain in one half of the head”), from Ancient Greek ἡμικρᾱνίᾰ (hēmikrāníă), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “hemi-, half”) + κρανίον (kraníon, “skull”) (from whence also cranium). Cognate to megrim and migraine, which also derive from the Latin.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the liver.
parole.testo: From Middle English epatik, from Late Latin hepaticus, from Ancient Greek ἡπατικός (hēpatikós, “of the liver”), from ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”).

parole.significato: Irregularly declined or inflected.
parole.testo: From Late Latin heteroclitus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερόκλιτος (heteróklitos), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + κλίνω (klínō, “lean, incline”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley-.

parole.significato: A flowering plant of the genus Hibiscus, especially Hibiscus syriacus, found in tropical to temperate regions, of some…
parole.testo: From Late Latin hibiscus, from Latin hibiscum, from Ancient Greek ἰβίσκος (ibískos, “marsh mallow”), probably ultimately from Gaulish.

parole.significato: A mythological creature with the front head and forelimbs of a horse and the rear of a fish.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hippocampus, from Ancient Greek ἱππόκαμπος (hippókampos, from ῐ̔́ππος (hĭ́ppos, “horse”) + κάμπος (kámpos, “sea-monster”)). The anatomy sense is so named from its resemblance to the seahorse. By surface analysis, hippo- + campus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to actors or acting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin histriōnicus (“pertaining to acting; scurrilous, shameful; wretched”), from Latin histriōnicus (“pertaining to acting and the theatre”), from histriō (“actor, player”) + -icus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’). By surface analysis, histrion + -ic.

parole.significato: Showing a degree of correspondence or similarity.
parole.testo: From Late Latin homologus, from Ancient Greek ὁμόλογος (homólogos, “agreeing, of one mind”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + λόγος (lógos, “reason, reckoning”). Compare homo- (“same”) and -ous (adjectival suffix). From 1655, in the mathematical sense. See also homolog, homologue.

parole.significato: To bristle in fear or horror; to have goose bumps or goose pimples.
parole.testo: From Late Latin horripilātus, perfect passive participle of horripilō (“(of hairs) to bristle”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from horreō (“to bristle, shiver, dread”) + pilus (“hair”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰers- (“to bristle”).

parole.significato: A real or fancied bristling of the hair of the head or body, resulting from disease, terror, chilliness, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin horripilatio, horripilationem.

parole.significato: Imbued with humanity.
parole.testo: First attested in 1551; borrowed from Late Latin hūmanātus, from hūmanus + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The bone of the upper arm.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin humerus, from umerus. Cognate with Spanish hombro (“shoulder”).

parole.significato: To cause to be ashamed; to injure the dignity and self-respect of.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin humiliātus, perfect passive participle of humiliō (“to abase, humble”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin humilis (“lowly, humble”), from humus (“ground; earth, soil”); see humble.

parole.significato: A member of a nomadic tribe (the Huns) who invaded Europe in the fourth century from Central Asia.
parole.testo: From Old English Hūnas, Hūne (both plural), from Late Latin Hunni, from Koine Greek Οὗννοι (Hoûnnoi), borrowed through Middle Iranian. Cognate with Old Norse húnir, Old High German Hunni. See also etymology of Xiongnu. Compare Sogdian 𐼶𐼴𐼻 (xwn), Sanskrit हूण (hūṇa), and 匈奴 (OC *hoŋ-nâ) (c. 318 BCE)

parole.significato: One of a race of people living in the extreme north, beyond the north wind.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hyperboreanus, cognate with Classical Latin hyperboreus, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβόρεος (huperbóreos), composed of ὑπέρ (hupér, “over”) + βόρειος (bóreios, “northern”). By surface analysis, nearly hyper- + boreal. See also Ὑπερβόρεοι (Huperbóreoi).

parole.significato: The symbol "‐", typically used to join two or more words to form a compound term, or to indicate that a word has been s…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin hyphen, from Ancient Greek ῠ̔φέν (hŭphén, “in one, as a single word”), univerbation of ῠ̔φ’ ἕν (hŭph’ hén, “under one”), from ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, “under”) + ἕν (hén, “one”), neuter of εἷς (heîs, “one”).

parole.significato: A term of endearment, often a diminutive; a pet name.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin hypocorisma, a loan from Ancient Greek ὑποκόρισμα (hupokórisma), ὑποκορισμός (hupokorismós, “pet name”), from ὑποκορίζεσθαι (hupokorízesthai), ὑποκορίζομαι (hupokorízomai, “to use a pet name; to act in a childish manner”), from ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, prefix indicating a small degree)

parole.significato: Like or pertaining to porcupines.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hystrix (genitive hystricis), a kind of porcupine.

parole.significato: Relating to, or having the characteristics of, an icon.
parole.testo: From Late Latin īconicus, from Ancient Greek εἰκονικός (eikonikós). By surface analysis, icon + -ic.

parole.significato: The actual existence supposed to correspond with an idea; the correlate in real existence to the idea as a thought or e…
parole.testo: From Late Latin ideatum. See idea.

parole.significato: Divination by idols, images or figures.
parole.testo: First element is from Late Latin idolum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”). Second element is from Latin -mantīa, ultimately from Ancient Greek μᾰντείᾱ (mănteíā). Equivalent to idol + -mancy.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to an illation.
parole.testo: From Late Latin illātīvus (“illative”), from Latin illātus, perfect passive participle of inferō (“carry or bring into somewhere; bury; conclude”), from in + ferō (“bear, carry; suffer”).

parole.significato: Not laudable; unpraiseworthy.
parole.testo: From Late Latin illaudabilis.

parole.significato: Tending to attract; enticing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin and Latin illecebrōsus (“attractive, enticing”) + English -ous (suffix forming adjectives denoting possession or presence of a quality, commonly in abundance). Illecebrōsus is derived from illecebra (“enticement, lure”) + -ōsus (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘full of’);

parole.significato: The act of immersing or the condition of being immersed.
parole.testo: From late Middle English, borrowed from Late Latin immersiō, immersiōnem (“dipping”).

parole.significato: The state or condition of being about to happen; imminent quality.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin imminentia.

parole.significato: To embody in bread, especially in the bread of the Eucharist.
parole.testo: From Late Latin impānātus, past participle of impānō.

parole.significato: the property of being impenitent, of lacking penitence, of not being regretful of wrongs done
parole.testo: From Late Latin impaenitentia.

parole.significato: To bring about; to put into practice; to carry out.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin implēmentum (“a filling up”), from Latin impleō (“to fill up”).

parole.significato: An act of filling; the state of being full.
parole.testo: From Late Latin implētiō (past participle of Latin impleō (“to fill up”) + -iō); see also implement.

parole.significato: Lacking the quality or ability of motion; as an inanimate object.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English inanimat(e), from Late Latin inanimātus, from Latin in- + animātus (“animated”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, in- + animate. The noun was derived by substantivization from the adjective, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: That cannot be apprehended; not apprehensible to or graspable by either body or mind.
parole.testo: Either from the Late Latin inapprehensibilis or formed in English as in- + apprehensible.

parole.significato: Without pause or stop; not ending, especially to the point of annoyance.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English incessaunte, from Late Latin incessāns, incessantem, from Latin in- + cessāns.

parole.significato: Not complete; not finished.
parole.testo: From Middle English incomplete, incompleet, from Late Latin incomplētus, from in- (“un-; not”) + complētus (“complete”), equivalent to in- (“not”) + complete.

parole.significato: Invisible.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin incōnspicuus. Equivalent to in- + conspicuous.

parole.significato: To include (something) as a part.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Late Latin incorporātus, perfect passive participle of incorporō (“to embody, to incorporate”), from in- (“in”) + corpus, corporis (“body”).

parole.significato: An evil spirit supposed to oppress people while asleep, especially to have sex with women as they sleep.
parole.testo: From Late Latin incubus, from Latin incubō (“nightmare, one who lies down on the sleeper”), from incubō (“to lie upon, to hatch”, from in- (“on”) + cubō (“to lie down”)).

parole.significato: To imply the guilt of; to blame or incriminate.
parole.testo: From Late Latin inculpo.

parole.significato: Blame; censure; crimination.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin inculpātiō.

parole.significato: Without limit; forever, or until further notice; not definite.
parole.testo: From Late Latin indēfīnītus. Morphologically in- + definite.

parole.significato: A pointer or index that indicates something.
parole.testo: From Late Latin indicātor (“one who points out”), from Latin indicō (“point out”). By surface analysis, indicate + -or; see indicate.

parole.significato: indescribable
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin indicibilis.

parole.significato: Native to a land, especially before colonization.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin indigenus (“native, born in a country”), from indi- (indu-), an old derivative of in (“in”), gen- the root of gignō (“give birth to”), and English -ous. Compare indigene, Ancient Greek ἐνδογενής (endogenḗs, “born in the house”), and the separately formed piecewise doublet en

parole.significato: Incapable of being subdued, overcome, or vanquished.
parole.testo: From Late Latin indomitābilis, from in- (“not”) + domitō, frequentative of domō (“to tame”). By surface analysis, in- + domitable.

parole.significato: The infinitive mood or mode (a grammatical mood).
parole.testo: From Middle English infenitife (“without end, in perpetuity”), from Late Latin īnfīnītīvus (“unlimited, indefinite”), from Latin īnfīnītus (“unlimited, infinite”). By surface analysis, infinite + -ive.

parole.significato: Something that provides a definitive characterization or description of the nature and attributes of a specified entity.
parole.testo: From Middle English enformacioun, informacioun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman informacioun, enformation, Old French information, from Latin īnfōrmātiō (“formation, conception; education”), from the participle stem of īnformāre (“to inform”). Equivalent to inform + -ation.

parole.significato: Not generated, self-existent.
parole.testo: First attested in 1656; borrowed from Late Latin ingenerātus, from in- (“not”) + generātus.

parole.significato: Synonym of hip bone (“one of two roughly symmetrical parts of the skeleton, each composed of the fused iliac, ischial,…
parole.testo: From innominate (“having no name, nameless, unnamed”, adjective) + bone (noun), possibly a calque of Late Latin os innōminātum. parole.significato: Someone who innovates; a creator of new ideas.
parole.testo: From Late Latin innovātor, from innovō; equivalent to innovate + -or.

parole.significato: Difficult or impossible to comprehend, fathom, or interpret.
parole.testo: Borrowed into late Middle English from Late Latin īnscrūtābilis, from in- (“not”) + scrūtō (“to examine”), corresponding to in- + scrutable

parole.significato: Not separate; together, united, undivided.
parole.testo: First attested in 1550; borrowed from Late Latin insēparātus. By surface analysis, in- (“not”) + separate.

parole.significato: An inspirer; one who inspires.
parole.testo: From Late Latin, from inspirare (“to inspire”) (from in- + spirare (“to breathe”)) + -tor.

parole.significato: To thicken a fluid, in the sense of making it more viscous, especially by boiling, evaporation, or condensation; to con…
parole.testo: Formed from Late Latin inspissātus (“thickened, having been made thick or thicker”), the perfect passive participle of inspissāre (“to thicken”).

parole.significato: To separate, detach, or isolate.
parole.testo: From Latin īnsula (“isle, island”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix) or from Late Latin īnsulātus (“made an island”), see etymology at -ate. parole.significato: The faculty of thinking, judging, abstract reasoning, and conceptual understanding; the cognitive faculty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin intellēctus (“understanding, intellect”), from Latin intellegō (“understand; reason”), from inter (“between, among”) + legō (“read”), with connotation of bind.

parole.significato: The characteristic of being intellectual; intellectual ability.
parole.testo: From intellectual + -ity, after Late Latin intellectualitas.

parole.significato: Capable of being interpreted or explained.
parole.testo: From the Late Latin interpretābilis, from interpretor; equivalent to interpret + -able; compare the obsolete French interpretable.

parole.significato: Asking or denoting a question.
parole.testo: From Late Latin interrogātīvus, equivalent to interrogate + -ive.

parole.significato: A formal question or set of questions submitted to opposing party to answer, generally governed by court rule.
parole.testo: From Late Latin; equivalent to interrogate + -ory (“pertaining to”), or more distantly inter- + rogatory.

parole.significato: Embezzlement.
parole.testo: From Late Latin interversiō.

parole.significato: Placed upon a throne; enthroned.
parole.testo: From Late Latin int(h)ronizātus, perfect participle participle of int(h)ronizō (“to inthronize”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To entitle.
parole.testo: From Late Latin intitulātus, past participle of intitulāre, whence intitule and entitle (obsolete intitle).

parole.significato: To stupefy by doping with chemical substances such as alcohol.
parole.testo: First attested in 1450, in Middle English; from Middle English intoxicaten, from intoxicat(e) (“(of a weapon or drug) smeared, anointed or filled with poison; (of a human being, animal) poisoned, intoxicated”, also used as the past participle of intoxicaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed fro

parole.significato: Introducing; giving a preview, idea or foretaste of.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin intrōductōrius, from Latin intrōductus.

parole.significato: One who invocates the spirits of the dead.
parole.testo: From Late Latin invocātor. By surface analysis, invocate + -or.

parole.significato: Without intention; unintentional.
parole.testo: From in- + voluntary, from Late Latin involontarius, from in + volontarius.

parole.significato: Characterized by or constituting (any kind of) irony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós). Compare Middle French, ironique, equivalent to irony + -ic.

parole.significato: Which cannot be refuted; clearly right, incontrovertible, indisputable, irrefutable.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin irrefrāgābilis (“irrefragable”) + English -able (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘able or fit to be done’). parole.significato: undeniable; unable to be disproved or refuted
parole.testo: From Late Latin irrefūtābilis, from ir- (“not”) + refūtābilis (“refutable”), from refūtō (“to refute”) + -bilis (“-able”), equivalent to ir- + refutable.

parole.significato: A creeping in.
parole.testo: From Late Latin irrēptiō, from Latin irrēpō (“to creep in”) + -tiō (suffix forming action nouns).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the erect phallus that was carried in bacchic processions.

parole.testo: From Middle English lavatorie, from Late Latin lavātōrium, from Latin lavāre (“to wash”) + -ium (forming places related to an activity). As a place to pan gold, via Spanish lavadero. Doublet of lavatorium and laver. See also lave.

parole.significato: A lay person who reads aloud certain religious texts in a church service.
parole.testo: From Middle English lector, lectoure, lectour, from Late Latin lēctor, from legō (“to read”). “Voice-over” sense probably adapted from Polish lektor. Doublet of lecture and lecturer.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia.

parole.significato: Transmigration of the soul, especially its reincarnation after death.

parole.significato: Mosaic.

parole.significato: A medicinal preparation of mummified human flesh; mummy.

parole.significato: The smooth muscle forming the wall of the uterus.

parole.significato: A swimming pool, especially an indoor one; a building housing one or more swimming pools.

parole.significato: An eight-year period.

parole.significato: Phantasmal, incorporeal.

parole.significato: The system of ecclesiastic governance by prelates or bishops; episcopacy, prelacy.

parole.significato: Refusing; denying; rejecting of the norm.
parole.testo: From the Late Latin recūsātīvus (“prohibitory”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to redhibition (the annulling of a sale).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin redhibitōrius, from redhibeō. For sense 2, compare French rédhibitoire.

parole.significato: A dining hall, especially in an institution such as a college or monastery.
parole.testo: Via Middle English refectori from Late Latin refectorium, from Latin reficere (“to remake, to rebuild”).

parole.significato: An automatic response to a simple stimulus which does not require mental processing.
parole.testo: From Late Latin reflexus, past participle of reflectere (“to bend back”), equivalent to re- + flex. Photography sense is from noun sense meaning “reflection”. Compare English reflect.

parole.significato: Able to be refuted, or shown to be false.
parole.testo: From Late Latin refūtābilis (“refutable”), equivalent to refute + -able.

parole.significato: To throw up or vomit; to eject what has previously been swallowed.
parole.testo: From Late Latin regurgitātus, past participle of regurgitāre, combined form of re- (“back”) + gurgitāre (“to engulf, flood”), from gurges (“whirlpool, gulf, sea, abyss”).

parole.significato: To say or do (something) for a second time, such as for emphasis.
parole.testo: Early 15th century, from Late Latin reiteratus, past participle of reiterare (“to repeat”) from re- (“again”) + iterare (“to repeat”) from iterum (“again”).

parole.significato: Resistance, struggle.
parole.testo: From (the stem of) Late Latin reluctatio, from the participle stem of Latin reluctārī.

parole.significato: An act of remembering long-past experiences, especially positive or pleasant ones, often fondly.
parole.testo: From Late Latin reminīscentiae (“remembrances”), from Latin reminīscēns, present active participle of reminīscor (“remember”); see reminiscent.

parole.significato: Of or relating to remembering; reminiscent.
parole.testo: From Late Latin reminiscentia + -al.

parole.significato: To object with in critical fashion; to express disapproval (with, against).
parole.testo: From (the participle stem of) Late Latin remōnstrō, from Latin re- + mōnstrō.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the kidneys.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin renalis, from Latin rēnēs (“kidneys”).

parole.significato: A repertoire.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin repertōrium. Doublet of repertoire.

parole.significato: Blameworthy, censurable, guilty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin reprehensibilis, from Latin reprehendo; equivalent to reprehend + -ible.

parole.significato: Synonym of reptile: creeping, crawling.
parole.testo: From Late Latin reptitius (“creeping”), corruption of Latin reperticius, from reptus (“crept, crawled”) + -īcius (“-itious”), from rēpere (“to creep, to crawl”), modified by English -ious, q.v. Cognate with repent, reptant, reptile, reptilious, surreptitious.

parole.significato: An act of rescinding: removing, taking away, or taking back.
parole.testo: 1651, Late Latin rescissio, from Latin rescindō (“to cut back”), from re- (“back”) + scindō (“to cut”).

parole.significato: Synonym of resolvable.
parole.testo: From Late Latin resolubilis, from Latin resolvō.

parole.significato: A chant or anthem recited after a reading in a church service; a respond.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English responsorie, from Late Latin respōnsōrium, from Latin respōnsus (“answered”), from the verb respondeō (“to answer”). Compare respond.

parole.significato: An act of retracting or withdrawing (a mistake, a statement, etc.); a retraction.

parole.significato: Someone who believes King Richard III was a just king, misrepresented by Tudor propaganda; a supporter of Richard III.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Ricardus (Latin form of Richard) + -ian.

parole.significato: A type of water snake formerly thought to poison water.
parole.testo: From Late Latin rinatrix (in Bartholomaeus Anglicus), apparently a misreading of Lucan 9.720 et natrix (“and the water snake”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin rīsōrius (“ridiculous, laughing”), clipping of mūsculus rīsōrius (“laughing muscle”).

parole.significato: A person with romantic character (a character like those of the knights in a mythic romance).
parole.testo: From romant + -ic, or borrowed from Late Latin romanticus (“(of a poem) having qualities of a romance”). Compare French romantique, which is borrowed from English. parole.significato: A disc.
parole.testo: From Late Latin rotella, diminutive of rota (“wheel”). Doublet of rowel.

parole.significato: One of the German reformers who rejected both the Roman and the Lutheran doctrine of the holy Eucharist.
parole.testo: From Late Latin sacramentarius, compare French sacramentaire.

parole.significato: A sacristan.
parole.testo: From Late Latin sacrista.

parole.significato: Able or intending to provide salvation or redemption.
parole.testo: From Late Latin salvificus, from Latin salvus (“saved, safe”) + facio (“make”).

parole.significato: giving salvation
parole.testo: From Late Latin salvificare (“to save”).

parole.significato: producing health; healing or curative
parole.testo: From Late Latin sānātōrius. See sanable.

parole.testo: From Late Latin sarcasmus, from Ancient Greek σαρκασμός (sarkasmós, “a sneer”), from σαρκάζω (sarkázō, “to gnash the teeth (in anger)”, literally “to strip off the flesh”), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”).

parole.significato: The act of saturating or the process of being saturated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin saturatio, saturationem.

parole.significato: Excessive sexual desire, found in a man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin satyriasis, from Ancient Greek σατυρίασις (saturíasis).

parole.significato: Having sides all unequal in length.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin scalēnus (“of unequal sides”), from Ancient Greek σκᾰληνός (skălēnós, “uneven, unequal”).

parole.significato: The rhythm or meter of a line or verse.
parole.testo: From Late Latin scansiōnem, accusative singular of scansiō (“the act of climbing”), from scandō (“to climb”).

parole.significato: To work roughly, or shape without finishing, as stone before leaving the quarry.
parole.testo: Compare Old French eskaper, eschapler (“to cut, hew”), Late Latin scapello. Compare scabble.

parole.significato: Either of the two large, flat, bones forming the back of the shoulder.
parole.testo: From Late Latin scapula (“shoulder”).

parole.significato: A student; one who studies at school or college, typically having a scholarship.

parole.significato: A scholar who writes commentary on the works of an author, especially one of the ancient commentators on classical auth…
parole.testo: From Late Latin scholiasta, from Byzantine Greek σχολιαστής (skholiastḗs), from σχολιάζειν (skholiázein), from Ancient Greek σχόλιον (skhólion).

parole.significato: shadow-boxing; fighting that is futile or make-believe
parole.testo: From Late Latin sciamachia, and its source, Hellenistic Ancient Greek σκιαμαχία (skiamakhía), from σκιά (skiá, “shadow”) + μάχη (mákhē, “battle”).

parole.significato: Neuralgia of the sciatic nerve, characterised by pain radiating down through the buttocks and the back of the thigh.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Late Latin sciatica, feminine of sciaticus, from Ancient Greek ἰσχιαδικός (iskhiadikós), the adjective of ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip”).

parole.significato: One who exhibits only superficial knowledge; a self-proclaimed expert with little real understanding.
parole.testo: From Late Latin sciolus + -ist. First attested at the beginning of the 17th century.

parole.significato: divination using shadows
parole.testo: From Late Latin sciomantia, from Ancient Greek σκιά (skiá, “shadow”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).

parole.significato: A longitudinal opening made by cutting; a cleft; a fissure.
parole.testo: From Late Latin scissura (“fissure”), from Latin scissurus (“about to split”), from scindo (“to split”).

parole.significato: A person born in or native to Scotland.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Scot, from Old English Sċottas (“people from Ireland, Irishmen”), from Late Latin Scōttī (see Scōtī for more). See Scoti.

parole.significato: An area of impaired or lost vision within a visual field otherwise in a good (or at least healthy) state.
parole.testo: From Late Latin scotoma, from Ancient Greek σκότωμα (skótōma), from σκότος (skótos, “darkness”). By surface analysis, scot- + -oma. The figurative sense is an extension from the literal sense, as if the mind, like an eye, cannot "see" certain things.

parole.significato: The second coat, or integument, of an ovule, lying within the primine.
parole.testo: From Late Latin secundinae (“afterbirth”), from Latin secundae (“the afterbirth”), shortened from secundae membranae "the second membranes", from secundus (“following, coming next”). See second.

parole.significato: producing seed
parole.testo: From Late Latin sēminifer (“carrying semen”).

parole.significato: A member of a modern people that speak a Semitic language.
parole.testo: From Sem, Shem + -ite, from Late Latin Sēm, from Ancient Greek Σήμ (Sḗm), from Biblical Hebrew שם (šēm). Compare German Semit, New Latin Sēmīta, French sémite.

parole.significato: The entire sensory apparatus of an organism.
parole.testo: From Late Latin sensōrium, from Latin sentiō (“feel, perceive”) + Latin -ōrium (suffix denoting a place for a particular function).

parole.significato: Inducing pleasurable or erotic sensations.
parole.testo: From Late Latin sensualis (“endowed with feeling, sensual”), from Latin sensus (“feeling, sense”).

parole.significato: A period of seven years.
parole.testo: From Late Latin septennium, from septennis (“7-year”) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: A silk gland, as in the silkworms.
parole.testo: Late Latin sericterium, from Ancient Greek σηρικόν (sērikón, “silk”).

parole.significato: Having six angles; hexagonal.
parole.testo: From Late Latin sexangulāris, from sexangulus. By surface analysis, sex- + -angular. Piecewise doublet of hexangular.

parole.significato: A person who keeps silent, especially from religious motives.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Late Latin silentiarius.

parole.significato: A disease of the lungs caused by the inhalation of crystalline silica dust.
parole.testo: From Late Latin silica + -osis.

parole.significato: A fine fiber excreted by the silkworm or other arthropod (such as a spider).

parole.significato: To place on or into a physical location.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin situātus, past participle of Medieval Latin situō (“to locate, place”), from Latin situs (“a site”).

parole.significato: A skeleton.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin sceletus, from Ancient Greek σκελετός (skeletós).

parole.significato: The act of a character speaking to themselves so as to reveal their thoughts to the audience.
parole.testo: 1595–1605; From Late Latin sōliloquium in the title of St. Augustine's Soliloquiorum libri duo ("Two Books of Soliloquies"), from sōlus (“only, sole”) + loquor (“to speak”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to alchemy; alchemical, especially regarding medicine.
parole.testo: From Late Latin spagyricus, from Ancient Greek σπάω (spáō, “I draw, pull”) + ἀγείρω (ageírō, “I assemble”).

parole.significato: spherical
parole.testo: From Late Latin sphaerālis.

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin sphinctēr (“the muscle of the anus”), from Ancient Greek σφῐγκτήρ (sphĭnktḗr, “lace, band; contractile muscle”), ultimately of Pre-Greek origin. Possibly related to sphinx (“the strangler”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the spine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin spīnālis (“of or belonging to the spine”), from spīna (“a prickle, spine”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, spine + -al.

parole.significato: Having a spine or spines.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin spīnēscēns, present participle of spīnēscō (“to become thorny”), from Latin spīna (“thorn”). By surface analysis, spine + -escent.

parole.significato: A minute spine or thorn.
parole.testo: Anglicized form of Late Latin spīnula, diminutive of Latin spīna (“a spine”). Compare French spinule.

parole.significato: Bad-tempered, irritable, peevish, spiteful, habitually angry.
parole.testo: The adjective form of spleen, borrowed from Late Latin spleneticus, from Latin splen. Anger was traditionally believed to originate from the fluids of the spleen.

parole.significato: Self-directed; happening or acting without external cause or instigation; proceeding from natural feeling, temperament,…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin spontāneus.

parole.significato: A case, capsule, or container in which spores are produced by an organism.
parole.testo: From Late Latin sporangium, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “seed”) + ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “vessel”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to tin mining, especially in Cornwall.
parole.testo: From Late Latin stannaria, from Latin stannum (“tin”). By surface analysis, stann- + -ary.

parole.testo: From Late Latin stapēs, stapedem (“stirrup”) + -otomy.

parole.significato: A receipt given by Jews on payment of debt.
parole.testo: From Late Latin starrum, from Hebrew שְׁטָר (šĕṭār).

parole.significato: The science of measuring the volume of solids or solid bodies.
parole.testo: From Late Latin, from Ancient Greek στερεομετρία (stereometría), from στερεός (stereós, “solid”).

parole.significato: A rule restricting behaviour or action.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin strictūra, from Latin strictus.

parole.significato: A person like an ostrich; someone who ignores facts or reality or someone who lacks responsibility.

parole.significato: Astonishingly great or large; huge; enormous.

parole.significato: Subordinate.
parole.testo: From Late Latin subalternus + -al.

parole.significato: An act of smiling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin subrisio (“smile”), from Latin subrīdeō (“to smile”).

parole.significato: Substitution of a different person in place of a creditor or claimant with respect to certain rights and duties.
parole.testo: From Late Latin subrogātiō, from sub- + rogātiō (“inquiry, request”); equivalent to sub- + rogation.

parole.significato: The process of subtracting a number from another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin subtractio, subtractionis. Can be decomposed to subtract + -ion.

parole.significato: An act of doing more than is required.

parole.significato: Existing, occurring, or located on the surface.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Late Latin superficiālis (“of or belonging to the surface”), from superficiēs (“top, surface”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: A person who works in a group, association, or public office without forming part of the regular staff (the numerary).
parole.testo: From Late Latin supernumerarius (“extra soldier added to a legion; supernumerary”), from super (“above; beyond”) + numerus (“number; collection, quantity”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives from nouns or numerals). The word is analysable as super- + numeral + -ary.

parole.significato: Of a natural number, being larger than another natural number by a unit fraction of that smaller number.
parole.testo: From Late Latin superparticulāris.

parole.significato: a foot-support for a crucified person, projecting from the base of the cross
parole.testo: From Late Latin suppedāneum, neuter of suppedāneus (“under the feet”), composed of sup- (“under”) + ped- (“foot”) + -aneus (“-aneous”).

parole.significato: Making up for deficiencies; supplementary; suppletory.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin suppletīvus.

parole.significato: A source of supply.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin suppletorius.

parole.significato: Likely to be affected by something.
parole.testo: From Late Latin susceptibilis, from Latin susceptus, from suscipiō.

parole.significato: The act of suspending, or the state of being suspended.

parole.significato: A brief summary of the major points of a written work, either as prose or as a table; an abridgment or condensation of…
parole.testo: From Late Latin synopsis, itself from Ancient Greek σύνοψις (súnopsis), from σύν (sún, “with or whole”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “view”) meaning whole view.

parole.significato: A constituent segment within a text, such as a word or a phrase that forms a syntactic unit.
parole.testo: From Late Latin syntagma, from Ancient Greek σύνταγμα (súntagma, “orderly arrangement”), from συντάσσω (suntássō, “arrange together”, “to order”).

parole.significato: A set of rules that govern how words are combined to form phrases and sentences.
parole.testo: Partly from Late Latin syntaxis and partly from its etymon, Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis), from σύν (sún, “together”) + τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”), from τάσσω (tássō, “to arrange”). Doublet of syntaxis.

parole.significato: Syntax.
parole.testo: From the Late Latin syntaxis, from the Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis). Doublet of syntax.

parole.significato: Carried out according to a planned, ordered procedure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin systēmaticus, from Koine Greek συστηματικός (sustēmatikós), from σύστημᾰ (sústēmă, “a composite; system”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, adjective suffix). Cognate with French systématique and Italian sistematico. By surface analysis, system + -atic.

parole.testo: From Late Latin sȳzygia (“a conjunction”), from Ancient Greek συζυγία (suzugía, “a union, a yoke, a pair”). This word was recognized as English in 1847 (in its astronomical meaning).

parole.significato: Having a flat (planar) horizontal surface at top.
parole.testo: From Late Latin tabulāris. By surface analysis, tabula + -ar, or, by surface analysis, table + -ar. Compare fabular.

parole.significato: To arrange in tabular form; to arrange into a table.

parole.significato: A pill, a tablet.
parole.testo: From Late Latin tabulāta (“thin board, plank, flooring”), or more likely a relatinized version of tablet through tabula.

parole.significato: Any of several shrubs, of the genus Tamarix, native to arid regions in Eurasia and Africa, often invasive in other arid…
parole.testo: From Late Latin tamariscus, from Latin tamarix.

parole.significato: Redundant use of words, a pleonasm, an unnecessary and tedious repetition.
parole.testo: From Late Latin tautologia, from Ancient Greek ταὐτολογία (tautología) from ταὐτός (tautós, “the same”) + λόγος (lógos, “explanation”). By surface analysis, tauto- + -logy.

parole.significato: Of or relating to construction or to architecture.
parole.testo: 1650s, in sense of building, from Late Latin tectonicus, from Ancient Greek τεκτονικός (tektonikós, “pertaining to building”), from Ancient Greek τέκτων (téktōn, “carpenter, joiner, maker”), from Proto-Indo-European *teḱ- (“to make”) (from which also texture). parole.significato: Of or relating to a temple.
parole.testo: From Late Latin templāris, from Latin templum (“temple”) + -āris, equivalent to temple + -ar.

parole.significato: A fan-shaped muscle which arises from the surface of the temporal fossa and converges to an aponeurosis which contracts…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin temporālis (“of or belonging to the temples of the head”), ellipsis of mūsculus temporālis (“the temporal muscle”). Doublet of temporal.

parole.significato: temporary
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin temporāneus (“timely”), derived from Latin tempor- (“time”).
